title: "Predicting performance"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

Coaches and athletes want to know what a step test means for the next race. Lactate thresholds are among the
strongest laboratory predictors of endurance performance, but a prediction for one athlete is less precise than the
correlations suggest. This article shows what lactater can predict, how sure the prediction is, and why the best
equation is the one you fit on your own athletes.

The short version:

* A step test predicts race speed to about +/- 10% in running (95% range) and time-trial power to about +/- 25 W in
  cycling, and only for tests run like those of the study the equation comes from.
* Every equation belongs to one threshold method: an equation fitted on IAT gives wrong numbers for LTP2.
* A recent race predicts the next one better than any step test ([Vickers & Vertosick, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y)).

## Running: 5 km to the marathon

The largest study of race prediction from a step test followed 427 competitive runners (88 women) who raced within 2
months of a treadmill test: 3-min stages, +2 km/h, a 2% grade, earlobe blood ([Roecker et al., 1998](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199810000-00014)). The speed at
the individual anaerobic threshold (IAT: the lowest lactate/speed ratio + 1.5 mmol/L, lactater's `IAT`) correlated
with mean race speed with r = 0.88 to 0.93, and each distance got its own straight line. A smaller study of 18 male
marathon runners related marathon speed to the speed at 4 mmol/L ([Sjödin & Jacobs, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2008-1034579)).

Here is a simulated runner tested with that protocol:

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)

runner <- tibble(
  intensity = c(0, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18),
  lactate = c(1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.6, 2.6, 4.6, 8.0)
)
results <- lactate_threshold(runner, intensity, lactate, sport = "running", plot = FALSE)
prediction <- predict_performance(results)
prediction
autoplot(prediction)
```

Each row gives the race time and the predicted mean race speed (`intensity`), each with its 95% range. The header repeats
the protocol of each source study, so you can check that your test matches it.

Read the ranges before the times. Roecker et al. did not report the error of their equations, so lactater derives
it from their tables: the SD of race speed times `sqrt(1 - r^2)`, about 5 to 6% of race speed, which makes a 95%
range of about +/- 10%. A predicted 3:09 marathon is anything from about 2:49 to 3:35. Two more details matter: the
equations predict the *best* race of the 2 months after the test (the authors kept the best result), and men and
women were pooled.

The two marathon estimates come from different thresholds and different studies, and they agree within a few
minutes here. That will not always be so; when they differ, the difference is part of the uncertainty.

## When the test was run differently

The runner in `lactate_tests` was tested on a treadmill at 0% grade, with +1 km/h steps after 16 km/h:

```{r}
tcd_results <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "running") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, sport = "running", plot = FALSE)

tcd_prediction <- predict_performance(tcd_results, method = "IAT")
tcd_prediction |>
  select(event, threshold, intensity, time)
```

A marathon in about 2:05 is close to the world record, for a runner described as trained. lactater warns twice: the steps
differ from the source protocol, and the IAT (20.4 km/h) lies above the runners Roecker et al. studied (about 10 to
20 km/h). Both matter:

* **The protocol moves the threshold.** Running on the flat costs less than at a 2% grade, so the same lactate
  appears at a higher speed. Smaller steps also move it: 1 instead of 2 km/h raised the speed at an individual
  anaerobic threshold by 6% ([Coen et al., 2001](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2001-11332)), and 6- instead of 3-min stages lowered the speed at 4 mmol/L from
  14.4 to 12.9 km/h ([Kuipers et al., 2003](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2003-42020)).
* **Outside the sample, a straight line is a guess.** At an IAT this high, the half-marathon equation even predicts
  a faster pace than the 10 km one.

lactater can read the steps from the data, but not the stage duration, the treadmill grade or the blood sample:
compare them with the protocol in the header yourself.

## Cycling: the 45-min time trial

For cycling, lactater fits its own equations on the open data of [Heuberger et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846): 48 well-trained men,
5-min stages of +25 W from 175 W, venous blood, and a 45-min time trial a week after the test
(`data-raw/performance_cycling.R`). Because the thresholds come from lactater itself, any of six methods can be used:

```{r}
cyclist_results <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "cycling_5min_no_rest") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)

cyclist_prediction <- predict_performance(cyclist_results)
cyclist_prediction
autoplot(cyclist_prediction)
```

This rider is one of the 48, so his prediction is not a fair test of the equations. On the whole sample, the
leave-one-out prediction errors (each rider predicted by the equation fitted without him) were:

| Predictor | Riders | r | Leave-one-out error | Time-trial power, % of the predictor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LTP2 | 39 | 0.88 | 12.3 W | 92 +/- 5% |
| IAT | 39 | 0.87 | 12.5 W | 95 +/- 6% |
| ModD<sub>max</sub> | 35 | 0.87 | 12.8 W | 94 +/- 4% |
| OBLA 4.0 | 33 | 0.84 | 12.9 W | 90 +/- 6% |
| Log-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub> | 38 | 0.86 | 13.8 W | 94 +/- 6% |
| D<sub>max</sub> | 39 | 0.79 | 16.2 W | 104 +/- 7% |
| Peak power of the step test | 39 | 0.92 | 10.4 W | 82 +/- 3% |

The last row is the lesson: the highest power of the step test predicted the time trial at least as well as any
lactate threshold, as other cycling studies found. A threshold is still the better guide to training, because it
marks an intensity domain; for predicting a race it adds little.

## Your own equation

The published equations apply to tests run like those of their studies. The most valid prediction comes from your
own athletes: test them with your protocol, collect a race result soon after each test, and fit the line yourself.
Any threshold, sport and protocol works. Here, 25 simulated runners of a lab that uses LTP2:

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
lab <- tibble(athlete = 1:25, ltp2 = round(rnorm(25, 15, 1.6), 1)) |>
  mutate(time_10km = round(10000 / ((0.6 + 1.01 * ltp2 + rnorm(25, 0, 0.45)) / 3.6)))
lab

own <- calibrate_performance(
  lab, threshold = "ltp2", performance = "time_10km", method = "LTP2",
  sport = "running", distance = 10000, protocol = "our lab: 3-min stages, +1 km/h, 1% grade, earlobe"
)
own
autoplot(own)
```

The header gives the equation, its correlation and its leave-one-out prediction error, the number that says how
well it will predict a new athlete. `predict_performance()` then uses your equation for new tests:

```{r}
predict_performance(results, equation = own)
```

With `distance`, race times are converted to the mean race intensity of the sport: speed for running and swimming,
and power for rowing (with the Concept2 relation between power and pace). For a cycling time trial, give the mean
power directly. In practice, run `lactate_threshold()` with `.by` on all your tests, keep the rows of your threshold
method, and join the race results by athlete.

## Race pace as a share of the threshold

How fast are races run, relative to a threshold? The answer depends on the threshold, the distance and the level of
the athlete, which is why it is shown here as a table to learn from, not as a predictor:

| Sport and race | Race intensity relative to the threshold | Population | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Running, 5 km | 117-120% of IAT | 427 competitive runners | [Roecker et al., 1998](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199810000-00014) (equations at IAT 14-17 km/h) |
| Running, 10 km | 109-110% of IAT | | |
| Running, half marathon | 104-107% of IAT | | |
| Running, marathon | 94-97% of IAT | | |
| Running, marathon | 87 +/- 6% of the speed at 4 mmol/L (78-98%) | 18 men, 2:22 to 4:12 | [Sjödin & Jacobs, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2008-1034579) |
| Running, marathon | about the speed at 2.5-3 mmol/L in a field test | 24 elite marathon runners | [Föhrenbach et al., 1987](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2008-1025633) |
| Cycling, 45-min time trial | 92% of LTP2, 90% of OBLA 4.0, 104% of D<sub>max</sub> | 48 well-trained men | [Heuberger et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846) (refitted) |
| Rowing, 2000 m | speed at 4 mmol/L = 89% of race speed | 13 club rowers | [Cosgrove et al., 1999](https://doi.org/10.1080/026404199365407) |
| Swimming, 400 m | 109% of the speed at 4 mmol/L | 15 competitive swimmers | [Ribeiro et al., 1990](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.24.3.196) |
| Swimming, 800-1500 m | 3.4% above the maximal lactate steady state | swimmers | [Hering & Stepan, 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.668123) |

In rowing, the power at 4 mmol/L is the threshold most often related to 2000 m performance, but maximal oxygen
uptake or peak power often predicted better ([Cosgrove et al., 1999](https://doi.org/10.1080/026404199365407); [Kilbey et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00796-4)). For rowing and swimming,
lactater has no published equation to offer; calibrate your own.

## A recent race is better

[Riegel (1981)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/27850427) described world-record times with `T2 = T1 x (D2 / D1)^b`, with a fatigue factor `b` of 1.077 for men
and 1.083 for women, and 1.05 to 1.06 for men aged 40 to 70. From a 40-min 10 km:

```{r}
riegel <- function(time, from, to, b) time * (to / from)^b
round(riegel(40, from = 10, to = c(5, 21.0975, 42.195), b = 1.077), 1)
```

The formula was well calibrated up to the half marathon in 2,303 recreational runners, but predicted a marathon at
least 10 minutes too fast for half of them ([Vickers & Vertosick, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y)). A step test is still worth doing: it tells
you why an athlete is fast, how to train, and how to pace when no recent race exists.
